newsitem.title: UK: Britain still planning for Zaire aid mission.
newsitem.headline: Britain still planning for Zaire aid mission.

text.p: A multinational military operation will probably still be needed to help refugees returning from Zaire to Rwanda, British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo said on Wednesday.
Plans for a large-scale intervention force have been scaled back since an estimated 500,000 refugees began a trek out of Zaire last Friday.
Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana said on Tuesday that there were "hardly any" Rwandan refugees left in Zaire and there was no need for the multinational peace force.
But Portillo told BBC radio: "I think a small number of troops anyway will be necessary on a multinational basis to help the Rwandans with taking people across the border."
Such a force could also help with an information campaign to convince other refugees that it was safe to return.
More than a million Hutus fled Rwanda in mid-1994 after it was overrun by Tutsi rebels, now in power, following the genocide of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus by Hutu extremists.
Portillo said British troops might still be needed to help refugees in Bukavu in southern Zaire.
Aid workers in the area said the exact whereabouts of hundreds of thousands of people were unknown.
"It is possible that there are still people in deep distress who need our help. So we'll go on planning the mission," the minister said.

Local people said that some 7,000 people from Bukavu camp who had tried to move northwards towards Goma last week to join the refugee flow home had been blocked by Hutus belonging to the Interahamwe militia halfway along Lake Kivu.
Portillo said he was despatching a reconnaissance aircraft to try to locate the refugees and assess what help was needed.

"We need much more information. I couldn't authorise the deployment of British troops until I have more information about that," he said from Moscow, where he is holding talks with Russian defence officials.
"I really can't say whether we are going to need a full military mission of the sort we were thinking of last week.
"We'll continue to plan on the basis that we might need it, but we can't commit until we know more about what's going on," he added.
Final decisions on a multinational deployment are expected after political talks in New York on Wednesday and a meeting of military planners in Stuttgart, Germany, on Friday.
